title: How Asia’s Surpluses Are Evolving
gist: Northeast Asian economies run large structural current account surpluses (Taiwan >17% of GDP) yet their currencies are deeply undervalued and trending weaker, because export dollar earnings were recycled into US-dollar foreign assets rather than converted, perpetuating undervaluation. Teaser only; the article's account of how this is evolving is paywalled.

insights.claim: Northeast Asian economies all run large structural current account surpluses above 3% of GDP, with Taiwan's exceeding 17% of GDP.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Surplus scale implies large latent appreciation pressure on regional currencies.
insights.quote: greater than 3% of their GDP (or greater than 17% in the case of Taiwan)

insights.claim: Despite large current account surpluses, Northeast Asian currencies are deeply undervalued by standard measures, contradicting conventional wisdom that surpluses drive appreciation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Valuation models based on current accounts have failed to predict Asian FX; mispricing could persist or snap back.
insights.quote: by any standard measure the currencies of Northeast Asia are deeply undervalued
insights.locator: The economies of Northeast Asia all

insights.claim: The structural trend for Northeast Asian currencies over the past few years has been toward further depreciation rather than appreciation.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Investors betting on Asian FX mean reversion have been fighting a persistent trend.
insights.quote: their structural trend over the last few years appears to be towards more depreciation

insights.claim: Northeast Asian economies recycled excess US dollar export earnings into purchasing foreign, mainly US-dollar-denominated, assets, which neutralized upward pressure on their currencies.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Asian capital outflows are a structural bid for USD assets; a change in recycling behavior would hit both Asian FX and US asset demand.
insights.quote: these economies recycled their excess US dollar earnings into purchasing foreign assets

insights.claim: The recycling of dollar surpluses into foreign assets kept Asian currencies undervalued, which in turn sustained export competitiveness and surpluses, creating a self-perpetuating cycle.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Breaking the cycle (e.g. via repatriation) would be a regime shift for Asian FX and global capital flows.
insights.quote: This recycling kept their currencies undervalued, so perpetuating the whole cycle.

insights.claim: Analysts have historically viewed the impact of current account balances on exchange rates through trade balances, a lens the article implies is insufficient because capital-account recycling dominates.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: FX analysis of surplus economies should track financial outflows, not just trade flows.
insights.quote: Historically, analysts have viewed the impact of current account balances on exchange rates through the prism of trade balances.
